1000595.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Eiríkr (“male given name”), with monophthongization of the original diphthong; compare Eirik, which preserves it. The Old Norse name is from Proto-Norse *Aiwa-rikiaʀ (“ever ruler”) or *Aina-rikiaʀ (“one ruler”). In the first analysis, the initial element is related to Proto-Germanic *aiwaz (“long time, eternity”); in the second, it is related to *ainaz (“one, single”). The second element continues Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“powerful, royal; ruler”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Erik, Danish Erik, Swedish Erik, Icelandic Eiríkur, Faroese Eirikur, English Eric, and German Er

1000851.etyen:
From Old Norse Stafangr, a compound of stafr + angr. Akin to Stavang. The meanings of the composite words are straightforward, but what exactly they refer to is unclear.
* angr (“bay, fjord”), in reference to a body of water. This could be Breiavatnet, Byfjorden, Hillevågsvatnet, Vågen , or Østervåg. Norwegian etymologist Inge Særheim sees Vågen, the inlet atop the mouth of which stands the Stavanger Cathedral, as the most likely candidate.
* stafr (“staff”), from Proto-Germanic *stabaz, relating to the straight and unbending shape of a landform. This could refer to the out-jutting headland on

1004947.etyen:
anorakk (“anorak”) + snor (“cord”), literally “anorak cord”. The first element, anorakk, ultimately reflects Greenlandic annoraaq (“anorak, fur overall”), from Proto-Inuit *atnuʀaaq (“clothing”), ultimately connected with Proto-Eskimo *atə- (“to put on”), although the precise formation of the Proto-Inuit word is uncertain. The second element, snor (“cord”), is probably from Middle Low German snor (“cord”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *snōrō (“rope, cord”).
Compare the parallel formation Danish anoraksnor (“anorak drawstring”).
